subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which SUVAT equation does NOT contain time t?
questions.explain: v² = u² + 2as relates velocity, acceleration and displacement without t.

questions.q: A material is described as 'stiff' if it has a:
questions.explain: Stiffness corresponds to a high Young modulus: large stress produces only small strain.

questions.q: A uniform 2.0 m beam weighs 40 N. Where does its weight effectively act?
options: At its centre, 1.0 m from each end
questions.explain: The weight of a uniform beam acts at its centre of mass, the geometric centre.

questions.q: Density is defined as:
questions.explain: Density ρ = mass ÷ volume, with units kg m⁻³.

questions.q: On a force–extension graph for a spring obeying Hooke's law, the gradient equals:
questions.explain: The gradient of a force–extension graph is the spring constant k.

questions.q: The moment of a force about a pivot is calculated as:
questions.explain: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action.

questions.q: The yield point of a ductile material marks where:
options: The wire returns to its original length
The material begins to extend rapidly with little extra force (plastic flow)
questions.explain: At the yield point the material yields, undergoing large plastic extension for little additional stress.

questions.q: An object is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance, how far does it fall in the first 2.0 s? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
Elastic deformation means that when the load is removed, the material:
questions.explain: Elastic deformation is fully recoverable: the material returns to its original shape.

questions.q: On a displacement–time graph, the gradient at a point represents:
questions.explain: The gradient of a displacement–time graph is the instantaneous velocity.

questions.q: Hooke's law states that, up to the limit of proportionality:
options: Extension is proportional to the applied force
Force is inversely proportional to extension
questions.explain: Hooke's law: extension is directly proportional to the applied force, F = kx.

questions.q: A force–extension graph for a metal wire shows a straight line then curves over before fracture. The straight portion corresponds to:
questions.explain: The initial straight-line region is the elastic region where Hooke's law holds.

questions.q: A couple consists of:
options: Two equal, parallel forces acting in the same direction
Two equal, antiparallel forces not acting in the same line
questions.explain: A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces whose lines of action differ, producing a turning effect.

questions.q: A force of 10 N acts at 30° above the horizontal. What is its horizontal component?
questions.explain: The horizontal component is the adjacent side, F cos30° ≈ 8.7 N.

questions.q: A 0.50 kg ball moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹ rebounds at 4.0 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The magnitude of the change in momentum is:
On a velocity–time graph, the area under the line represents:
questions.explain: The area under a velocity–time graph gives the displacement.

questions.q: Tensile strain is defined as:
questions.explain: Strain ε = extension ÷ original length and is a dimensionless ratio.

questions.q: A 0.15 kg cricket ball is struck and its velocity changes by 30 m s⁻¹ over 0.010 s. The average force on the ball is:
The limit of proportionality on a force–extension graph is the point beyond which:
options: Force is no longer proportional to extension
questions.explain: Beyond the limit of proportionality, extension is no longer directly proportional to force (Hooke's law fails).

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally from a cliff. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity:
questions.explain: With no horizontal force, the horizontal velocity stays constant throughout the flight.

questions.q: Plastic deformation is characterised by:
options: A permanent change in shape after the load is removed
questions.explain: Plastic deformation leaves a permanent extension once the load is removed.

questions.q: A wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries a tension of 40 N. The tensile stress is:
Tensile stress is defined as:
questions.explain: Stress σ = force ÷ cross-sectional area, with units Pa (N m⁻²).

questions.q: The spring constant k represents:
options: The stiffness — force needed per unit extension
questions.explain: k is the stiffness, the force required to produce unit extension (N m⁻¹).

questions.q: The SI unit of the Young modulus is the same as that of:
questions.explain: Strain is dimensionless, so the Young modulus has the units of stress, the pascal.

questions.q: A steel wire and a rubber band are both stretched. Compared with steel, rubber typically has a:
questions.explain: Rubber is far more easily stretched than steel, so it has a much lower Young modulus.

questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explain: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, whereas speed, distance and mass are scalars.

questions.q: A ductile material is one that:
options: Can undergo large plastic deformation and be drawn into wires
Does not obey Hooke's law at all
questions.explain: Ductile materials (e.g. copper) deform plastically a great deal and can be drawn into wires.

questions.q: A projectile is launched and lands at the same height. At the highest point of its path, its vertical velocity is:
questions.explain: At the peak the vertical component of velocity is momentarily zero.

questions.q: The elastic limit of a material is the point beyond which:
options: The material no longer returns to its original length when unloaded
questions.explain: Beyond the elastic limit, deformation becomes permanent (plastic).
